---
title: "Your first look at DAS data"
guide-section: Tutorial
---

In this tutorial you make a small directory of DAS data, open it in the viewer, draw an annotation on it, and read that annotation back in Python. It takes about ten minutes.

## Install dastor

dastor needs DASCore's `dev` branch, so install both from GitHub:

```bash
pip install \
  "dascore @ git+https://github.com/DASDAE/dascore@dev" \
  "dastor @ git+https://github.com/DASDAE/dastor"
```

## Make some data

Save this as `make_data.py` and run it with `python make_data.py`. It writes DASCore's example data as three files, one per patch:

```python
from pathlib import Path

import dascore as dc

folder = Path("das_example")
folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
for number, patch in enumerate(dc.get_example_spool("random_das", time_gap=0)):
    patch.io.write(folder / f"patch_{number}.h5", "DASDAE")
```

You now have a directory, `das_example`, holding 24 seconds of random data.

## Open the viewer

```bash
dastor browse das_example
```

Your browser opens on the viewer, showing the data as an image: time across, distance up. Turn the mouse wheel over it to zoom, and drag to move around. Press `w` to see the whole recording again.

## Draw an annotation

1. Press `4`, the box tool.
2. Drag a box over part of the data.
3. A label box opens beside it: type `noise` and press Enter.

The box is saved as you draw it, in an annotation set named `annotations`. dastor keeps it beside the data, in `das_example_annotations`.

## Read it back in Python

Stop the server with Ctrl+C. Sets are kept under their owner's name, which for `dastor browse` is your user name on this machine. Read yours with DASCore:

```python
import getpass

import dascore as dc

sets = dc.annotations(f"das_example_annotations/{getpass.getuser()}")
print(sets)
```

The summary shows one annotation and one feature: the box you drew, with the distance and time it covers. `sets.features` lists its features, with the label `noise`.
